20.2 · Why Is the Way a Government Is Organized Important?

Who Decides, and Where?

Government systems and environmental policy sit on two separate questions. Click a country for a real example.

Federal SystemsStates or provinces have powers independent of the central government (US, Canada, India, Brazil). Environmental policy fragmented across levels.
AuthoritarianPower concentrated in one person or small group. Can mandate rapid environmental changes, as China did with car restrictions and industrial regulations.
DemocraticPublic plays a significant role in decision-making. Policy changes are slower but more durable, built on public consensus.
Unitary SystemsCentral government alone directs policy (France, China). More consistent national environmental standards but less local flexibility.

20.4 · How Are Environmental Policies Made?

How Are Environmental Policies Made?

Politics pits people with different perspectives in power struggles, and this can make it difficult for both sides to ‘win.’ Understanding how policy is made is essential to influencing it.

The volley: carbon rules for power plants, 2007 to 2022
Pushing for actionPushing back
  1. 2007
    Massachusetts v. EPAStates and environmental groups win at the Supreme Court, 5 to 4: greenhouse gases are “air pollutants” the Clean Air Act covers.
  2. 2009
    Endangerment findingEPA finds that greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare, opening the door to rules.
  3. 2015
    Clean Power PlanEPA sets carbon limits for power plants, after 4.3 million public comments.
  4. 2016
    Supreme Court stayCoal states and companies sue. In February the Court freezes the plan before it takes effect.
  5. 2019
    Repeal and replaceA new administration repeals the plan and issues a narrower rule (Affordable Clean Energy).
  6. 2022
    West Virginia v. EPAThe Court rules 6 to 3 that EPA lacked the authority for a plan like the original one.
  7. 2022
    Congress answersSeven weeks later, the Inflation Reduction Act writes greenhouse gases into the Clean Air Act and funds clean energy.

Massachusetts v. EPA, 549 U.S. 497 (2007); EPA endangerment finding (Dec. 2009); Clean Power Plan (Aug. 2015; EPA: 4.3 million comments); Supreme Court stay (Feb. 9, 2016); Affordable Clean Energy rule (June 2019); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (June 30, 2022); Inflation Reduction Act (Aug. 16, 2022).

    20.6 · How Did Important US Environmental Policies Develop?

    Headlines That Built the EPA

    Final editionThe Daily RecordThe 1950s

    Chemical Age Arrives

    Factories, suburbs and new synthetic pesticides spread with no national pollution law

    Before the 1970s: rapid post-war development and synthetic chemical use with no national pollution policy.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordSeptember 27, 1962

    A Biologist Warns of a “Silent Spring”

    Rachel Carson’s book on pesticides becomes a best seller

    Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962): credited with sparking public concern about pesticides and pollution, contributing directly to the creation of the EPA in 1970.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordJune 23, 1969

    Oil on the Coast, Fire on the River

    Santa Barbara’s blowout and Cleveland’s burning Cuyahoga make national news

    An offshore oil blowout coats the Santa Barbara coast in January. In June, Ohio’s Cuyahoga River, slick with industrial waste, catches fire. Both make national news.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordApril 22, 1970

    Millions Turn Out for the First Earth Day

    Rallies and teach-ins in cities and on campuses across the country

    Graduate student Denis Hayes organizes the first Earth Day. About 20 million Americans take part.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordDecember 2, 1970

    New Federal Agency Will Police Pollution

    The Environmental Protection Agency opens; the Clean Air Act is signed before New Year’s

    EPA established 1970. The Clean Air Act follows the same month.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordOctober 18, 1972

    Congress Overrides Veto on Clean Water

    Months after the EPA bans DDT for most uses

    EPA bans DDT for most uses, and the Clean Water Act (1972) becomes law when Congress overrides a presidential veto.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordDecember 28, 1973

    Endangered Species Act Signed Into Law

    The third landmark law in four years

    The Endangered Species Act (1973) completes the run. Clean Air Act (1970), Clean Water Act (1972), and Endangered Species Act (1973) followed in rapid succession.

    Final editionThe Daily RecordSince the 1970s

    Two Pillars of US Environmental Law

    Pollution control and natural resources

    Natural resource policy: the federal government owns 28% of US land, and controls resource use through national forests, parks, and BLM lands. These policy areas, pollution control and natural resources, remain the two major pillars of US environmental law.

    The clipping file
    On the books
    EPAClean Air ActDDT banClean Water ActEndangered Species Act

    20.6 · Pollution Control Policies: The Major Laws

    Follow the Pollution

    1Clean Air Act (1970)Air

    Regulates air pollutants from mobile and stationary sources. Established national ambient air quality standards.

    How it worksEPA sets national limits for common air pollutants, and each state writes a plan to meet them. Tailpipes (mobile) and smokestacks (stationary) both face emission standards.
    ExampleLead was phased out of US gasoline under the Act; the final ban on leaded gas for cars took effect on January 1, 1996.
    2Clean Water Act (1972)Water

    Regulates pollution discharges into US waters. Sets water quality standards for surface waters.

    How it worksDischarging pollution from a pipe or ditch into a river, lake, or coastal water is illegal without a permit, and the permit sets the limits.
    ExampleCongress passed it in 1972 over a presidential veto, three years after the Cuyahoga River fire.
    3RCRA (1976)Waste on the move

    Resource Conservation and Recovery Act: governs hazardous and solid waste generation, transport, and disposal.

    How it worksHazardous waste is tracked “from cradle to grave”: every shipment travels with a manifest from the plant that made it to the site that disposes of it.
    ExampleYour town’s landfill must meet RCRA design rules for liners and groundwater monitoring.
    4CERCLA / Superfund (1980)Land already poisoned

    Comprehensive Environmental Response Act: funds cleanup of contaminated hazardous waste sites.

    How it worksThe parties responsible for contamination must pay for its cleanup; the fund pays when they cannot be found.
    ExampleLove Canal, Niagara Falls, New York: homes and a school stood over about 21,000 tons of buried chemical waste. A 1978 federal emergency there pushed Congress to pass Superfund.
    © 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.

    20.6 · Did the Laws Work?

    One Year, Two Americas

    Sources & fine print

    Every number on this slide, cited

    1. US EPA (2011). The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020 (Second Prospective Study). Central estimate: the 1990 Amendments prevent ~230,000 adult premature deaths in the year 2020 alone; annual benefits ~$2.0 trillion vs. ~$65 billion compliance costs (~30:1; sensitivity range ~3:1–90:1).
    2. US EPA (1997). The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act, 1970 to 1990 (Retrospective Study). ~205,000 premature deaths avoided in 1990 alone; total 1970–1990 benefits $5.6–49.4 trillion (mean $22.2T) vs. ~$0.5 trillion costs.
    3. CDC NHANES / US EPA. After the Clean-Air-Act-driven phase-out of leaded gasoline, average blood-lead levels in young US children fell more than 90% from the late-1970s baseline (~15 µg/dL).
    4. Keiser, D.A. & Shapiro, J.S. (2019). “Consequences of the Clean Water Act and the Demand for Water Quality.” Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(1): 349–396. Most pollution measures fell sharply after 1972; the share of waters violating fishable standards declined ~12 percentage points; ~$650B (2014$) flowed through municipal treatment grants, ~$1T total abatement spending. They also note official benefit tallies omit most health and ecosystem values.
    5. US Fish & Wildlife Service (2020). Bald eagle population update: 417 known breeding pairs in the lower 48 in 1963 → an estimated 71,467 pairs by 2019. Bald eagle delisted 2007.
    6. Greenwald, N., Suckling, K.F., Hartl, B. & Mehrhoff, L. (2019). “Extinction and the U.S. Endangered Species Act.” PeerJ 7:e6803: the ESA prevented an estimated 291 extinctions through 2019; more than 99% of listed species survive.

    Honest caveats: benefit estimates rely on valuing statistical lives and are uncertain (hence the published ranges); Clean Water Act benefits are the hardest to price because drinking-water health effects and ecosystem services were largely excluded from official cost–benefit tallies.

    20.7 · How Are Environmental Issues Addressed Internationally?

    Pollution Without Passports

    UNEP 1972WHO 1948WTO 1995IPCC 1988Click a marker on the map.
    • Environmental impacts cross national borders: acid rain, ocean pollution, and greenhouse gases ignore political boundaries. International cooperation is essential, but sovereignty makes it difficult.
    • Intergovernmental organizations (IGOs): UNEP, WHO, WTO, formed by member countries to facilitate cooperation.
    • The IPCC convenes thousands of experts to assess climate science and inform policy, which is a model of evidence-based international governance.

    20.7 · International Agreements: How They Work in the US

    Treaties, Agreements, and the Senate

    67votes needed to ratify a treaty: two-thirds of the Senate
    • US treaties require 2/3 Senate ratification, a high bar that has prevented US participation in several international environmental agreements.
    • Executive agreements (not requiring Senate approval) can achieve some international commitments but are reversible by the next president (as seen with the Paris Agreement).

    20.7 · The Montreal Protocol: A Success Story

    Why the Montreal Protocol Worked

    The 1987 Montreal Protocol is considered the world’s most successful international environmental agreement: the ozone layer is on track to recover by mid-century.

    197countries ratified
    83–0US Senate vote, 1988
    ~2066Antarctic ozone back to 1980 levels
    • Scientific consensus was clear: CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone, increasing UV radiation and skin cancer.
    • Economic alternatives to CFCs already existed, making compliance relatively painless for industry.
    • Universal participation: 197 countries ratified, including all major CFC producers.
    • Lessons for climate policy: agreements succeed when the science is clear, alternatives are available, and costs are shared equitably.

    Ozone hole: NASA Ozone Watch (mean area, Sept. 7 to Oct. 13), via Our World in Data; 1995 not measured. Recovery: WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion (2022). Senate: Voteview.

    Sources & assumptions

    Where these numbers come from

    Measured

    1. California Air Resources Board (2019). SB 1014 Clean Miles Standard: 2018 Base-year Emissions Inventory Report. 38.5% of ride-hail miles had no passenger; 1.55 passengers per fare; 301 g CO₂ per passenger-mile against 203 for California’s average car.
    2. Henao, A. & Marshall, W. E. (2019). The impact of ride-hailing on vehicle miles traveled. Transportation 46(6): 2173–2194. At least 40.8% of ride-hail miles in Denver were driven empty; ride-hailing led to about 83.5% more vehicle miles than if it had not existed.
    3. Millard-Ball, A. (2019). The autonomous vehicle parking problem. Transport Policy 75: 99–108. Self-driving cars that cruise rather than pay to park could more than double vehicle travel to, from and within dense urban cores.
    4. U.S. Federal Highway Administration (2018). Summary of Travel Trends: 2017 National Household Travel Survey, Table 16. 1.67 people per vehicle-mile for all trips; 1.18 for trips to and from work.
    5. New York State Department of Taxation and Finance. Congestion surcharge, Manhattan south of 96th Street: $2.75 a for-hire trip, $2.50 a taxi trip, $0.75 a shared (pool) trip.
    6. Bureau of Public Roads (1964). Traffic Assignment Manual. The speed-and-volume curve used by planners: travel time rises with (volume / capacity)4.

    Assumed in the model

    • A mid-size downtown with 20,000 self-driving car trips a weekday, 3 miles each way inside the core.
    • Riders stay for an errand (1 hour, 40% of trips), an afternoon (3 hours, 25%) or a workday (8 hours, 35%).
    • An empty car can circle slowly (6 mph), park in a lot half a mile away ($3 an hour, at most $25 a day), or drive home (10 miles each way). It costs $0.12 a mile to run. Owners differ, so each picks the cheapest option most of the time, not every time.
    • A limit on empty miles rules out any choice that drives more empty miles than the limit; the car parks instead.
    • Without a subsidy 10% of travelers share rides; each $1 per shared ride makes sharing more popular (about 30% at $2.40).
    • Today, with people parking their own cars, the downtown streets run at 90% of capacity and 22.8 mph on average.
    • CO₂: 287 g per car-mile, today’s California ride-hail fleet (from CARB’s 301 g per passenger-mile).

    Government: How Can Policy Influence Sustainability?

    Policy
    Authoritative decisions (laws, regulations, court rulings) guiding behavior
    Legitimacy
    Widely shared belief that government authority is appropriately held
    Federal System
    States have some powers independent of the central government
    SMDP vs. PR
    Winner-take-all vs. proportional representation electoral systems
    Interest Group
    Organizations formed to influence government on shared interests
    Prescriptive Regulation
    Mandate on what can/cannot be done: manufacturers must comply
    Montreal Protocol
    1987 treaty that successfully phased out ozone-depleting CFCs
    Paris Agreement
    2015 non-binding national emissions targets for climate change

    20.5 · How Are Policies Designed to Influence Behavior?

    Cap-and-Trade: Let the Market Find the Cheap Cuts

    You run a factory that pollutes, and so does everyone. Round 1 has no cap: pollute freely. Then a pollution cap arrives and gets stricter every round. Clean up and go under your cap to earn credits you can sell, or keep polluting over the cap and buy credits from cleaner factories. Watch what happens to total pollution, and to costs, as the cap falls.
    Waiting for the instructor to open the market…
    🏭 Your factory emits 5 tons of pollution. Cleanup costs YOU $? per ton — and your tech can clean at most 4 tons (no factory can reach zero).
    🧹 Reduce pollution (cleanup costs your rate per ton)
    0tons (max 4)
    🎫 Buy or sell credits ◀ sell  ·  buy ▶ (go under the cap to earn credits you can sell)
    0
    Leaderboard
    ROUND 1 of 4
    Pollution emitted, round by round
    ▮ tons emitted ╌ the cap$ = class total cost
    Round 1 has no pollution cap — polluting is free. Then a cap on pollution arrives and gets stricter every round. Watch total pollution fall — and watch each factory pick its cheaper path: clean up, go under the cap, and sell credits… or keep polluting over the cap and buy them.
    Cap-and-trade: the regulator sets a pollution CAP per factory and lowers it over time. Emit UNDER your cap and you earn credits to sell; emit OVER it and you must buy credits from cleaner factories. Each factory picks whichever is cheaper — cleaning up or buying — so the cap's pollution cut happens at the lowest possible total cost.
